case_info.scenario: A 6-month-old girl presented with yellowish papules and nodules on the face and trunk (Figure 1A). The skin lesions appeared 2 months prior, initially on the scalp, then gradually spread to the trunk. Physical examination revealed yellowish papules and nodules on the scalp, face, abdomen, back, and perineum. No fever, lymphadenopathy, or hepatosplenomegaly was noted. Her medical and family histories were unremarkable, and she demonstrated age-appropriate developmental milestones. Results of laboratory tests, including blood cell count and liver and kidney functions, were within normal limits. After obtaining informed consent from the parents, a punch biopsy of an abdominal lesion was performed for histopathological examination (Figure 1B).
case_info.caption: A, Multiple yellowish papules and nodules on the scalp and face. B, Panoramic view of the histopathologic image demonstrating sheets of histiocytes with foamy cytoplasm and scattered Touton giant cells in the papillary dermis without epidermotropism or emperipolesis (hematoxylin-eosin).
case_info.explanation: D. Anaplastic lymphoma kinase–positive histiocytosis Histopathologic examination revealed sheets of histiocytes with foamy cytoplasm and scattered Touton giant cells in the papillary dermis. No epidermotropism or emperipolesis was observed. Immunohistochemical staining results were negative for S100, CD1a, CD207, andBRAFV600E alteration, while positive for CD68, CD163, and anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK) (Figure 2). Chest radiology revealed no specific abnormalities. Abdominal sonography showed no hepatosplenomegaly and normal hepatobiliary system. Neonatal neurosonography revealed no obvious brain tumor. Positron emission tomography showed no noteworthy resorption except for a nodule on the left forehead. Genetic analysis yielded positive results for theDCTN1::ALKfusion gene. The clinical, histopathological, and molecular findings were consistent with a diagnosis of ALK-positive histiocytosis with single-system involvement. ALK-positive histiocytosis is a novel histiocytic proliferative disorder characterized by a unique gene translocation involving the fusion of theALKgene with various partners.1Infants with systemic manifestations such as pallor, anemia, thrombocytopenia, and hepatosplenomegaly were initially reported in a case series in 2008.2The disease has since expanded to include patients older than 40 years with local or systemic involvement.3Subsequent studies have validated the distinct clinicopathological and molecular features of ALK-positive histiocytosis, including the characteristicKIF5B::ALKgene fusion, neurological manifestations, and favorable responses to ALK inhibitors.4Currently, ALK-positive histiocytosis is recognized as a distinct histiocytic neoplasm according to the World Health Organization classification system.5 ALK-positive histiocytosis has a female predominance, in contrast with the male predominance observed in Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH) and juvenile xanthogranuloma (JXG).4A comprehensive understanding of ALK-positive histiocytosis requires systemic surveys, leading to further subcategorization into group 1A (multisystem involvement, including the liver, spleen, and hematopoietic systems), group 1B (multisystem involvement, encompassing the nervous systems, lungs, bone, skin, and lymph nodes), and group 2 (single-system involvement).4Of note, group 2 usually involves the skin or nervous systems and often requires surgical removal. ALK-positive histiocytosis and JXG have potential similarities in clinical manifestations and histopathological findings.6,7Both ALK-positive histiocytosis and JXG exhibit positive staining for CD68 and CD163, and lesional tumor cells in ALK-positive histiocytosis are positive for ALK staining.7,8Molecular testing for ALK rearrangements should be performed to confirm the diagnosis of ALK-positive histiocytosis, particularly in patients presenting with multiple lesions with atypical histiocytic proliferation.4,8In addition to the commonly observedKIF5B::ALKgene fusion, documented cases include other gene fusions, includingDCTN1::ALK,CLTC::ALK, andTPM3::ALK.4,8It is noteworthy that patients with ALK-positive staining but no ALK rearrangements may not benefit from ALK inhibition.4In unresectable cases, disease control may require the use of chemotherapy, radiotherapy, and ALK inhibitors, such as crizotinib, alectinib, or lorlatinib.4,8 Cutaneous histiocytoses encompass a diverse group of diseases characterized by the accumulation of cells in the skin exhibiting cytological and phenotypic features of macrophages or dendritic cells.7In LCH, cutaneous lesions typically present as erythematous vesicles, pustules, or papulonodules. Histopathological examination reveals monomorphous, medium-sized histiocytes containing a pink and kidney-shaped nucleus, often accompanied by epidermal exocytosis. Definite diagnosis of LCH relies on positive immunostaining for S100, CD1a, and CD207,7all of which were negative in the present patient. Rosai-Dorfman disease typically manifests as widespread, erythematous to brownish papulonodules in children. Systemic symptoms may occur and include fever, lymphadenopathy, and anemia. Histopathological examination reveals signs of emperipolesis, a feature not observed in the present patient. Immunostaining results for Rosai-Dorfman disease may be positive for S100, CD68, and CD163 and negative for CD1a and CD207.7Erdheim-Chester disease (ECD) typically affects adults, with characteristic cutaneous manifestations of yellow-brown papules or plaques on the face or trunk.1,8,9Classic histopathologic features of ECD include foamy histiocytes with small nuclei, Touton giant cells, and extensive fibrosis, and it is characterized by positive immunostaining for CD68 and CD163 and negative staining for CD1a and CD207.9﻿BRAFV600E alteration may also be present in ECD.8,9 This case outlines a patient presenting with typical clinical and histopathological features of ALK-positive histiocytosis with single-system involvement, as confirmed by positive results for theDCTN1::ALKfusion gene. Treatment options such as vinblastine/prednisolone-based chemotherapy or crizotinib were suggested, but the patient’s family expressed hesitation. Therefore, the patient was treated with prednisolone, 4 mg, twice daily and topical hydrocortisone ointment, with periodic follow-up for outcome evaluation. Although diagnosis of this unique entity is rare, it is critical for physicians to perform a thorough systemic examination and implement appropriate treatment.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: D. Anaplastic lymphoma kinase–positive histiocytosis Histopathologic examination revealed sheets of histiocytes with foamy cytoplasm and scattered Touton giant cells in the papillary dermis. No epidermotropism or emperipolesis was observed. Immunohistochemical staining results were negative for S100, CD1a, CD207, andBRAFV600E alteration, while positive for CD68, CD163, and anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK) (Figure 2). Chest radiology revealed no specific abnormalities. Abdominal sonography showed no hepatosplenomegaly and normal hepatobiliary system. Neonatal neurosonography revealed no obvious brain tumor. Positron emission tomography showed no noteworthy resorption except for a nodule on the left forehead. Genetic analysis yielded positive results for theDCTN1::ALKfusion gene. The clinical, histopathological, and molecular findings were consistent with a diagnosis of ALK-positive histiocytosis with single-system involvement. ALK-positive histiocytosis is a novel histiocytic proliferative disorder characterized by a unique gene translocation involving the fusion of theALKgene with various partners.1Infants with systemic manifestations such as pallor, anemia, thrombocytopenia, and hepatosplenomegaly were initially reported in a case series in 2008.2The disease has since expanded to include patients older than 40 years with local or systemic involvement.3Subsequent studies have validated the distinct clinicopathological and molecular features of ALK-positive histiocytosis, including the characteristicKIF5B::ALKgene fusion, neurological manifestations, and favorable responses to ALK inhibitors.4Currently, ALK-positive histiocytosis is recognized as a distinct histiocytic neoplasm according to the World Health Organization classification system.5 ALK-positive histiocytosis has a female predominance, in contrast with the male predominance observed in Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH) and juvenile xanthogranuloma (JXG).4A comprehensive understanding of ALK-positive histiocytosis requires systemic surveys, leading to further subcategorization into group 1A (multisystem involvement, including the liver, spleen, and hematopoietic systems), group 1B (multisystem involvement, encompassing the nervous systems, lungs, bone, skin, and lymph nodes), and group 2 (single-system involvement).4Of note, group 2 usually involves the skin or nervous systems and often requires surgical removal. ALK-positive histiocytosis and JXG have potential similarities in clinical manifestations and histopathological findings.6,7Both ALK-positive histiocytosis and JXG exhibit positive staining for CD68 and CD163, and lesional tumor cells in ALK-positive histiocytosis are positive for ALK staining.7,8Molecular testing for ALK rearrangements should be performed to confirm the diagnosis of ALK-positive histiocytosis, particularly in patients presenting with multiple lesions with atypical histiocytic proliferation.4,8In addition to the commonly observedKIF5B::ALKgene fusion, documented cases include other gene fusions, includingDCTN1::ALK,CLTC::ALK, andTPM3::ALK.4,8It is noteworthy that patients with ALK-positive staining but no ALK rearrangements may not benefit from ALK inhibition.4In unresectable cases, disease control may require the use of chemotherapy, radiotherapy, and ALK inhibitors, such as crizotinib, alectinib, or lorlatinib.4,8 Cutaneous histiocytoses encompass a diverse group of diseases characterized by the accumulation of cells in the skin exhibiting cytological and phenotypic features of macrophages or dendritic cells.7In LCH, cutaneous lesions typically present as erythematous vesicles, pustules, or papulonodules. Histopathological examination reveals monomorphous, medium-sized histiocytes containing a pink and kidney-shaped nucleus, often accompanied by epidermal exocytosis. Definite diagnosis of LCH relies on positive immunostaining for S100, CD1a, and CD207,7all of which were negative in the present patient. Rosai-Dorfman disease typically manifests as widespread, erythematous to brownish papulonodules in children. Systemic symptoms may occur and include fever, lymphadenopathy, and anemia. Histopathological examination reveals signs of emperipolesis, a feature not observed in the present patient. Immunostaining results for Rosai-Dorfman disease may be positive for S100, CD68, and CD163 and negative for CD1a and CD207.7Erdheim-Chester disease (ECD) typically affects adults, with characteristic cutaneous manifestations of yellow-brown papules or plaques on the face or trunk.1,8,9Classic histopathologic features of ECD include foamy histiocytes with small nuclei, Touton giant cells, and extensive fibrosis, and it is characterized by positive immunostaining for CD68 and CD163 and negative staining for CD1a and CD207.9﻿BRAFV600E alteration may also be present in ECD.8,9 This case outlines a patient presenting with typical clinical and histopathological features of ALK-positive histiocytosis with single-system involvement, as confirmed by positive results for theDCTN1::ALKfusion gene. Treatment options such as vinblastine/prednisolone-based chemotherapy or crizotinib were suggested, but the patient’s family expressed hesitation. Therefore, the patient was treated with prednisolone, 4 mg, twice daily and topical hydrocortisone ointment, with periodic follow-up for outcome evaluation. Although diagnosis of this unique entity is rare, it is critical for physicians to perform a thorough systemic examination and implement appropriate treatment.

case_info.explanation: D. Anaplastic lymphoma kinase–positive histiocytosis Histopathologic examination revealed sheets of histiocytes with foamy cytoplasm and scattered Touton giant cells in the papillary dermis. No epidermotropism or emperipolesis was observed. Immunohistochemical staining results were negative for S100, CD1a, CD207, andBRAFV600E alteration, while positive for CD68, CD163, and anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK) (Figure 2). Chest radiology revealed no specific abnormalities. Abdominal sonography showed no hepatosplenomegaly and normal hepatobiliary system. Neonatal neurosonography revealed no obvious brain tumor. Positron emission tomography showed no noteworthy resorption except for a nodule on the left forehead. Genetic analysis yielded positive results for theDCTN1::ALKfusion gene. The clinical, histopathological, and molecular findings were consistent with a diagnosis of ALK-positive histiocytosis with single-system involvement. ALK-positive histiocytosis is a novel histiocytic proliferative disorder characterized by a unique gene translocation involving the fusion of theALKgene with various partners.1Infants with systemic manifestations such as pallor, anemia, thrombocytopenia, and hepatosplenomegaly were initially reported in a case series in 2008.2The disease has since expanded to include patients older than 40 years with local or systemic involvement.3Subsequent studies have validated the distinct clinicopathological and molecular features of ALK-positive histiocytosis, including the characteristicKIF5B::ALKgene fusion, neurological manifestations, and favorable responses to ALK inhibitors.4Currently, ALK-positive histiocytosis is recognized as a distinct histiocytic neoplasm according to the World Health Organization classification system.5 ALK-positive histiocytosis has a female predominance, in contrast with the male predominance observed in Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH) and juvenile xanthogranuloma (JXG).4A comprehensive understanding of ALK-positive histiocytosis requires systemic surveys, leading to further subcategorization into group 1A (multisystem involvement, including the liver, spleen, and hematopoietic systems), group 1B (multisystem involvement, encompassing the nervous systems, lungs, bone, skin, and lymph nodes), and group 2 (single-system involvement).4Of note, group 2 usually involves the skin or nervous systems and often requires surgical removal. ALK-positive histiocytosis and JXG have potential similarities in clinical manifestations and histopathological findings.6,7Both ALK-positive histiocytosis and JXG exhibit positive staining for CD68 and CD163, and lesional tumor cells in ALK-positive histiocytosis are positive for ALK staining.7,8Molecular testing for ALK rearrangements should be performed to confirm the diagnosis of ALK-positive histiocytosis, particularly in patients presenting with multiple lesions with atypical histiocytic proliferation.4,8In addition to the commonly observedKIF5B::ALKgene fusion, documented cases include other gene fusions, includingDCTN1::ALK,CLTC::ALK, andTPM3::ALK.4,8It is noteworthy that patients with ALK-positive staining but no ALK rearrangements may not benefit from ALK inhibition.4In unresectable cases, disease control may require the use of chemotherapy, radiotherapy, and ALK inhibitors, such as crizotinib, alectinib, or lorlatinib.4,8 Cutaneous histiocytoses encompass a diverse group of diseases characterized by the accumulation of cells in the skin exhibiting cytological and phenotypic features of macrophages or dendritic cells.7In LCH, cutaneous lesions typically present as erythematous vesicles, pustules, or papulonodules. Histopathological examination reveals monomorphous, medium-sized histiocytes containing a pink and kidney-shaped nucleus, often accompanied by epidermal exocytosis. Definite diagnosis of LCH relies on positive immunostaining for S100, CD1a, and CD207,7all of which were negative in the present patient. Rosai-Dorfman disease typically manifests as widespread, erythematous to brownish papulonodules in children. Systemic symptoms may occur and include fever, lymphadenopathy, and anemia. Histopathological examination reveals signs of emperipolesis, a feature not observed in the present patient. Immunostaining results for Rosai-Dorfman disease may be positive for S100, CD68, and CD163 and negative for CD1a and CD207.7Erdheim-Chester disease (ECD) typically affects adults, with characteristic cutaneous manifestations of yellow-brown papules or plaques on the face or trunk.1,8,9Classic histopathologic features of ECD include foamy histiocytes with small nuclei, Touton giant cells, and extensive fibrosis, and it is characterized by positive immunostaining for CD68 and CD163 and negative staining for CD1a and CD207.9﻿BRAFV600E alteration may also be present in ECD.8,9 This case outlines a patient presenting with typical clinical and histopathological features of ALK-positive histiocytosis with single-system involvement, as confirmed by positive results for theDCTN1::ALKfusion gene. Treatment options such as vinblastine/prednisolone-based chemotherapy or crizotinib were suggested, but the patient’s family expressed hesitation. Therefore, the patient was treated with prednisolone, 4 mg, twice daily and topical hydrocortisone ointment, with periodic follow-up for outcome evaluation. Although diagnosis of this unique entity is rare, it is critical for physicians to perform a thorough systemic examination and implement appropriate treatment.

case_info.explanation: D. Anaplastic lymphoma kinase–positive histiocytosis Histopathologic examination revealed sheets of histiocytes with foamy cytoplasm and scattered Touton giant cells in the papillary dermis. No epidermotropism or emperipolesis was observed. Immunohistochemical staining results were negative for S100, CD1a, CD207, andBRAFV600E alteration, while positive for CD68, CD163, and anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK) (Figure 2). Chest radiology revealed no specific abnormalities. Abdominal sonography showed no hepatosplenomegaly and normal hepatobiliary system. Neonatal neurosonography revealed no obvious brain tumor. Positron emission tomography showed no noteworthy resorption except for a nodule on the left forehead. Genetic analysis yielded positive results for theDCTN1::ALKfusion gene. The clinical, histopathological, and molecular findings were consistent with a diagnosis of ALK-positive histiocytosis with single-system involvement. ALK-positive histiocytosis is a novel histiocytic proliferative disorder characterized by a unique gene translocation involving the fusion of theALKgene with various partners.1Infants with systemic manifestations such as pallor, anemia, thrombocytopenia, and hepatosplenomegaly were initially reported in a case series in 2008.2The disease has since expanded to include patients older than 40 years with local or systemic involvement.3Subsequent studies have validated the distinct clinicopathological and molecular features of ALK-positive histiocytosis, including the characteristicKIF5B::ALKgene fusion, neurological manifestations, and favorable responses to ALK inhibitors.4Currently, ALK-positive histiocytosis is recognized as a distinct histiocytic neoplasm according to the World Health Organization classification system.5 ALK-positive histiocytosis has a female predominance, in contrast with the male predominance observed in Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH) and juvenile xanthogranuloma (JXG).4A comprehensive understanding of ALK-positive histiocytosis requires systemic surveys, leading to further subcategorization into group 1A (multisystem involvement, including the liver, spleen, and hematopoietic systems), group 1B (multisystem involvement, encompassing the nervous systems, lungs, bone, skin, and lymph nodes), and group 2 (single-system involvement).4Of note, group 2 usually involves the skin or nervous systems and often requires surgical removal. ALK-positive histiocytosis and JXG have potential similarities in clinical manifestations and histopathological findings.6,7Both ALK-positive histiocytosis and JXG exhibit positive staining for CD68 and CD163, and lesional tumor cells in ALK-positive histiocytosis are positive for ALK staining.7,8Molecular testing for ALK rearrangements should be performed to confirm the diagnosis of ALK-positive histiocytosis, particularly in patients presenting with multiple lesions with atypical histiocytic proliferation.4,8In addition to the commonly observedKIF5B::ALKgene fusion, documented cases include other gene fusions, includingDCTN1::ALK,CLTC::ALK, andTPM3::ALK.4,8It is noteworthy that patients with ALK-positive staining but no ALK rearrangements may not benefit from ALK inhibition.4In unresectable cases, disease control may require the use of chemotherapy, radiotherapy, and ALK inhibitors, such as crizotinib, alectinib, or lorlatinib.4,8 Cutaneous histiocytoses encompass a diverse group of diseases characterized by the accumulation of cells in the skin exhibiting cytological and phenotypic features of macrophages or dendritic cells.7In LCH, cutaneous lesions typically present as erythematous vesicles, pustules, or papulonodules. Histopathological examination reveals monomorphous, medium-sized histiocytes containing a pink and kidney-shaped nucleus, often accompanied by epidermal exocytosis. Definite diagnosis of LCH relies on positive immunostaining for S100, CD1a, and CD207,7all of which were negative in the present patient. Rosai-Dorfman disease typically manifests as widespread, erythematous to brownish papulonodules in children. Systemic symptoms may occur and include fever, lymphadenopathy, and anemia. Histopathological examination reveals signs of emperipolesis, a feature not observed in the present patient. Immunostaining results for Rosai-Dorfman disease may be positive for S100, CD68, and CD163 and negative for CD1a and CD207.7Erdheim-Chester disease (ECD) typically affects adults, with characteristic cutaneous manifestations of yellow-brown papules or plaques on the face or trunk.1,8,9Classic histopathologic features of ECD include foamy histiocytes with small nuclei, Touton giant cells, and extensive fibrosis, and it is characterized by positive immunostaining for CD68 and CD163 and negative staining for CD1a and CD207.9﻿BRAFV600E alteration may also be present in ECD.8,9 This case outlines a patient presenting with typical clinical and histopathological features of ALK-positive histiocytosis with single-system involvement, as confirmed by positive results for theDCTN1::ALKfusion gene. Treatment options such as vinblastine/prednisolone-based chemotherapy or crizotinib were suggested, but the patient’s family expressed hesitation. Therefore, the patient was treated with prednisolone, 4 mg, twice daily and topical hydrocortisone ointment, with periodic follow-up for outcome evaluation. Although diagnosis of this unique entity is rare, it is critical for physicians to perform a thorough systemic examination and implement appropriate treatment.

   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.

   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.

case_info.explanation: D. Anaplastic lymphoma kinase–positive histiocytosis Histopathologic examination revealed sheets of histiocytes with foamy cytoplasm and scattered Touton giant cells in the papillary dermis. No epidermotropism or emperipolesis was observed. Immunohistochemical staining results were negative for S100, CD1a, CD207, andBRAFV600E alteration, while positive for CD68, CD163, and anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK) (Figure 2). Chest radiology revealed no specific abnormalities. Abdominal sonography showed no hepatosplenomegaly and normal hepatobiliary system. Neonatal neurosonography revealed no obvious brain tumor. Positron emission tomography showed no noteworthy resorption except for a nodule on the left forehead. Genetic analysis yielded positive results for theDCTN1::ALKfusion gene. The clinical, histopathological, and molecular findings were consistent with a diagnosis of ALK-positive histiocytosis with single-system involvement. ALK-positive histiocytosis is a novel histiocytic proliferative disorder characterized by a unique gene translocation involving the fusion of theALKgene with various partners.1Infants with systemic manifestations such as pallor, anemia, thrombocytopenia, and hepatosplenomegaly were initially reported in a case series in 2008.2The disease has since expanded to include patients older than 40 years with local or systemic involvement.3Subsequent studies have validated the distinct clinicopathological and molecular features of ALK-positive histiocytosis, including the characteristicKIF5B::ALKgene fusion, neurological manifestations, and favorable responses to ALK inhibitors.4Currently, ALK-positive histiocytosis is recognized as a distinct histiocytic neoplasm according to the World Health Organization classification system.5 ALK-positive histiocytosis has a female predominance, in contrast with the male predominance observed in Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH) and juvenile xanthogranuloma (JXG).4A comprehensive understanding of ALK-positive histiocytosis requires systemic surveys, leading to further subcategorization into group 1A (multisystem involvement, including the liver, spleen, and hematopoietic systems), group 1B (multisystem involvement, encompassing the nervous systems, lungs, bone, skin, and lymph nodes), and group 2 (single-system involvement).4Of note, group 2 usually involves the skin or nervous systems and often requires surgical removal. ALK-positive histiocytosis and JXG have potential similarities in clinical manifestations and histopathological findings.6,7Both ALK-positive histiocytosis and JXG exhibit positive staining for CD68 and CD163, and lesional tumor cells in ALK-positive histiocytosis are positive for ALK staining.7,8Molecular testing for ALK rearrangements should be performed to confirm the diagnosis of ALK-positive histiocytosis, particularly in patients presenting with multiple lesions with atypical histiocytic proliferation.4,8In addition to the commonly observedKIF5B::ALKgene fusion, documented cases include other gene fusions, includingDCTN1::ALK,CLTC::ALK, andTPM3::ALK.4,8It is noteworthy that patients with ALK-positive staining but no ALK rearrangements may not benefit from ALK inhibition.4In unresectable cases, disease control may require the use of chemotherapy, radiotherapy, and ALK inhibitors, such as crizotinib, alectinib, or lorlatinib.4,8 Cutaneous histiocytoses encompass a diverse group of diseases characterized by the accumulation of cells in the skin exhibiting cytological and phenotypic features of macrophages or dendritic cells.7In LCH, cutaneous lesions typically present as erythematous vesicles, pustules, or papulonodules. Histopathological examination reveals monomorphous, medium-sized histiocytes containing a pink and kidney-shaped nucleus, often accompanied by epidermal exocytosis. Definite diagnosis of LCH relies on positive immunostaining for S100, CD1a, and CD207,7all of which were negative in the present patient. Rosai-Dorfman disease typically manifests as widespread, erythematous to brownish papulonodules in children. Systemic symptoms may occur and include fever, lymphadenopathy, and anemia. Histopathological examination reveals signs of emperipolesis, a feature not observed in the present patient. Immunostaining results for Rosai-Dorfman disease may be positive for S100, CD68, and CD163 and negative for CD1a and CD207.7Erdheim-Chester disease (ECD) typically affects adults, with characteristic cutaneous manifestations of yellow-brown papules or plaques on the face or trunk.1,8,9Classic histopathologic features of ECD include foamy histiocytes with small nuclei, Touton giant cells, and extensive fibrosis, and it is characterized by positive immunostaining for CD68 and CD163 and negative staining for CD1a and CD207.9﻿BRAFV600E alteration may also be present in ECD.8,9 This case outlines a patient presenting with typical clinical and histopathological features of ALK-positive histiocytosis with single-system involvement, as confirmed by positive results for theDCTN1::ALKfusion gene. Treatment options such as vinblastine/prednisolone-based chemotherapy or crizotinib were suggested, but the patient’s family expressed hesitation. Therefore, the patient was treated with prednisolone, 4 mg, twice daily and topical hydrocortisone ointment, with periodic follow-up for outcome evaluation. Although diagnosis of this unique entity is rare, it is critical for physicians to perform a thorough systemic examination and implement appropriate treatment.

case_info.explanation: D. Anaplastic lymphoma kinase–positive histiocytosis Histopathologic examination revealed sheets of histiocytes with foamy cytoplasm and scattered Touton giant cells in the papillary dermis. No epidermotropism or emperipolesis was observed. Immunohistochemical staining results were negative for S100, CD1a, CD207, andBRAFV600E alteration, while positive for CD68, CD163, and anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK) (Figure 2). Chest radiology revealed no specific abnormalities. Abdominal sonography showed no hepatosplenomegaly and normal hepatobiliary system. Neonatal neurosonography revealed no obvious brain tumor. Positron emission tomography showed no noteworthy resorption except for a nodule on the left forehead. Genetic analysis yielded positive results for theDCTN1::ALKfusion gene. The clinical, histopathological, and molecular findings were consistent with a diagnosis of ALK-positive histiocytosis with single-system involvement. ALK-positive histiocytosis is a novel histiocytic proliferative disorder characterized by a unique gene translocation involving the fusion of theALKgene with various partners.1Infants with systemic manifestations such as pallor, anemia, thrombocytopenia, and hepatosplenomegaly were initially reported in a case series in 2008.2The disease has since expanded to include patients older than 40 years with local or systemic involvement.3Subsequent studies have validated the distinct clinicopathological and molecular features of ALK-positive histiocytosis, including the characteristicKIF5B::ALKgene fusion, neurological manifestations, and favorable responses to ALK inhibitors.4Currently, ALK-positive histiocytosis is recognized as a distinct histiocytic neoplasm according to the World Health Organization classification system.5 ALK-positive histiocytosis has a female predominance, in contrast with the male predominance observed in Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH) and juvenile xanthogranuloma (JXG).4A comprehensive understanding of ALK-positive histiocytosis requires systemic surveys, leading to further subcategorization into group 1A (multisystem involvement, including the liver, spleen, and hematopoietic systems), group 1B (multisystem involvement, encompassing the nervous systems, lungs, bone, skin, and lymph nodes), and group 2 (single-system involvement).4Of note, group 2 usually involves the skin or nervous systems and often requires surgical removal. ALK-positive histiocytosis and JXG have potential similarities in clinical manifestations and histopathological findings.6,7Both ALK-positive histiocytosis and JXG exhibit positive staining for CD68 and CD163, and lesional tumor cells in ALK-positive histiocytosis are positive for ALK staining.7,8Molecular testing for ALK rearrangements should be performed to confirm the diagnosis of ALK-positive histiocytosis, particularly in patients presenting with multiple lesions with atypical histiocytic proliferation.4,8In addition to the commonly observedKIF5B::ALKgene fusion, documented cases include other gene fusions, includingDCTN1::ALK,CLTC::ALK, andTPM3::ALK.4,8It is noteworthy that patients with ALK-positive staining but no ALK rearrangements may not benefit from ALK inhibition.4In unresectable cases, disease control may require the use of chemotherapy, radiotherapy, and ALK inhibitors, such as crizotinib, alectinib, or lorlatinib.4,8 Cutaneous histiocytoses encompass a diverse group of diseases characterized by the accumulation of cells in the skin exhibiting cytological and phenotypic features of macrophages or dendritic cells.7In LCH, cutaneous lesions typically present as erythematous vesicles, pustules, or papulonodules. Histopathological examination reveals monomorphous, medium-sized histiocytes containing a pink and kidney-shaped nucleus, often accompanied by epidermal exocytosis. Definite diagnosis of LCH relies on positive immunostaining for S100, CD1a, and CD207,7all of which were negative in the present patient. Rosai-Dorfman disease typically manifests as widespread, erythematous to brownish papulonodules in children. Systemic symptoms may occur and include fever, lymphadenopathy, and anemia. Histopathological examination reveals signs of emperipolesis, a feature not observed in the present patient. Immunostaining results for Rosai-Dorfman disease may be positive for S100, CD68, and CD163 and negative for CD1a and CD207.7Erdheim-Chester disease (ECD) typically affects adults, with characteristic cutaneous manifestations of yellow-brown papules or plaques on the face or trunk.1,8,9Classic histopathologic features of ECD include foamy histiocytes with small nuclei, Touton giant cells, and extensive fibrosis, and it is characterized by positive immunostaining for CD68 and CD163 and negative staining for CD1a and CD207.9﻿BRAFV600E alteration may also be present in ECD.8,9 This case outlines a patient presenting with typical clinical and histopathological features of ALK-positive histiocytosis with single-system involvement, as confirmed by positive results for theDCTN1::ALKfusion gene. Treatment options such as vinblastine/prednisolone-based chemotherapy or crizotinib were suggested, but the patient’s family expressed hesitation. Therefore, the patient was treated with prednisolone, 4 mg, twice daily and topical hydrocortisone ointment, with periodic follow-up for outcome evaluation. Although diagnosis of this unique entity is rare, it is critical for physicians to perform a thorough systemic examination and implement appropriate treatment.

case_info.explanation: D. Anaplastic lymphoma kinase–positive histiocytosis Histopathologic examination revealed sheets of histiocytes with foamy cytoplasm and scattered Touton giant cells in the papillary dermis. No epidermotropism or emperipolesis was observed. Immunohistochemical staining results were negative for S100, CD1a, CD207, andBRAFV600E alteration, while positive for CD68, CD163, and anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK) (Figure 2). Chest radiology revealed no specific abnormalities. Abdominal sonography showed no hepatosplenomegaly and normal hepatobiliary system. Neonatal neurosonography revealed no obvious brain tumor. Positron emission tomography showed no noteworthy resorption except for a nodule on the left forehead. Genetic analysis yielded positive results for theDCTN1::ALKfusion gene. The clinical, histopathological, and molecular findings were consistent with a diagnosis of ALK-positive histiocytosis with single-system involvement. ALK-positive histiocytosis is a novel histiocytic proliferative disorder characterized by a unique gene translocation involving the fusion of theALKgene with various partners.1Infants with systemic manifestations such as pallor, anemia, thrombocytopenia, and hepatosplenomegaly were initially reported in a case series in 2008.2The disease has since expanded to include patients older than 40 years with local or systemic involvement.3Subsequent studies have validated the distinct clinicopathological and molecular features of ALK-positive histiocytosis, including the characteristicKIF5B::ALKgene fusion, neurological manifestations, and favorable responses to ALK inhibitors.4Currently, ALK-positive histiocytosis is recognized as a distinct histiocytic neoplasm according to the World Health Organization classification system.5 ALK-positive histiocytosis has a female predominance, in contrast with the male predominance observed in Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH) and juvenile xanthogranuloma (JXG).4A comprehensive understanding of ALK-positive histiocytosis requires systemic surveys, leading to further subcategorization into group 1A (multisystem involvement, including the liver, spleen, and hematopoietic systems), group 1B (multisystem involvement, encompassing the nervous systems, lungs, bone, skin, and lymph nodes), and group 2 (single-system involvement).4Of note, group 2 usually involves the skin or nervous systems and often requires surgical removal. ALK-positive histiocytosis and JXG have potential similarities in clinical manifestations and histopathological findings.6,7Both ALK-positive histiocytosis and JXG exhibit positive staining for CD68 and CD163, and lesional tumor cells in ALK-positive histiocytosis are positive for ALK staining.7,8Molecular testing for ALK rearrangements should be performed to confirm the diagnosis of ALK-positive histiocytosis, particularly in patients presenting with multiple lesions with atypical histiocytic proliferation.4,8In addition to the commonly observedKIF5B::ALKgene fusion, documented cases include other gene fusions, includingDCTN1::ALK,CLTC::ALK, andTPM3::ALK.4,8It is noteworthy that patients with ALK-positive staining but no ALK rearrangements may not benefit from ALK inhibition.4In unresectable cases, disease control may require the use of chemotherapy, radiotherapy, and ALK inhibitors, such as crizotinib, alectinib, or lorlatinib.4,8 Cutaneous histiocytoses encompass a diverse group of diseases characterized by the accumulation of cells in the skin exhibiting cytological and phenotypic features of macrophages or dendritic cells.7In LCH, cutaneous lesions typically present as erythematous vesicles, pustules, or papulonodules. Histopathological examination reveals monomorphous, medium-sized histiocytes containing a pink and kidney-shaped nucleus, often accompanied by epidermal exocytosis. Definite diagnosis of LCH relies on positive immunostaining for S100, CD1a, and CD207,7all of which were negative in the present patient. Rosai-Dorfman disease typically manifests as widespread, erythematous to brownish papulonodules in children. Systemic symptoms may occur and include fever, lymphadenopathy, and anemia. Histopathological examination reveals signs of emperipolesis, a feature not observed in the present patient. Immunostaining results for Rosai-Dorfman disease may be positive for S100, CD68, and CD163 and negative for CD1a and CD207.7Erdheim-Chester disease (ECD) typically affects adults, with characteristic cutaneous manifestations of yellow-brown papules or plaques on the face or trunk.1,8,9Classic histopathologic features of ECD include foamy histiocytes with small nuclei, Touton giant cells, and extensive fibrosis, and it is characterized by positive immunostaining for CD68 and CD163 and negative staining for CD1a and CD207.9﻿BRAFV600E alteration may also be present in ECD.8,9 This case outlines a patient presenting with typical clinical and histopathological features of ALK-positive histiocytosis with single-system involvement, as confirmed by positive results for theDCTN1::ALKfusion gene. Treatment options such as vinblastine/prednisolone-based chemotherapy or crizotinib were suggested, but the patient’s family expressed hesitation. Therefore, the patient was treated with prednisolone, 4 mg, twice daily and topical hydrocortisone ointment, with periodic follow-up for outcome evaluation. Although diagnosis of this unique entity is rare, it is critical for physicians to perform a thorough systemic examination and implement appropriate treatment.

case_info.scenario: A 6-month-old girl presented with yellowish papules and nodules on the face and trunk (Figure 1A). The skin lesions appeared 2 months prior, initially on the scalp, then gradually spread to the trunk. Physical examination revealed yellowish papules and nodules on the scalp, face, abdomen, back, and perineum. No fever, lymphadenopathy, or hepatosplenomegaly was noted. Her medical and family histories were unremarkable, and she demonstrated age-appropriate developmental milestones. Results of laboratory tests, including blood cell count and liver and kidney functions, were within normal limits. After obtaining informed consent from the parents, a punch biopsy of an abdominal lesion was performed for histopathological examination (Figure 1B).
case_info.caption: A, Multiple yellowish papules and nodules on the scalp and face. B, Panoramic view of the histopathologic image demonstrating sheets of histiocytes with foamy cytoplasm and scattered Touton giant cells in the papillary dermis without epidermotropism or emperipolesis (hematoxylin-eosin).
case_info.explanation: D. Anaplastic lymphoma kinase–positive histiocytosis Histopathologic examination revealed sheets of histiocytes with foamy cytoplasm and scattered Touton giant cells in the papillary dermis. No epidermotropism or emperipolesis was observed. Immunohistochemical staining results were negative for S100, CD1a, CD207, andBRAFV600E alteration, while positive for CD68, CD163, and anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK) (Figure 2). Chest radiology revealed no specific abnormalities. Abdominal sonography showed no hepatosplenomegaly and normal hepatobiliary system. Neonatal neurosonography revealed no obvious brain tumor. Positron emission tomography showed no noteworthy resorption except for a nodule on the left forehead. Genetic analysis yielded positive results for theDCTN1::ALKfusion gene. The clinical, histopathological, and molecular findings were consistent with a diagnosis of ALK-positive histiocytosis with single-system involvement. ALK-positive histiocytosis is a novel histiocytic proliferative disorder characterized by a unique gene translocation involving the fusion of theALKgene with various partners.1Infants with systemic manifestations such as pallor, anemia, thrombocytopenia, and hepatosplenomegaly were initially reported in a case series in 2008.2The disease has since expanded to include patients older than 40 years with local or systemic involvement.3Subsequent studies have validated the distinct clinicopathological and molecular features of ALK-positive histiocytosis, including the characteristicKIF5B::ALKgene fusion, neurological manifestations, and favorable responses to ALK inhibitors.4Currently, ALK-positive histiocytosis is recognized as a distinct histiocytic neoplasm according to the World Health Organization classification system.5 ALK-positive histiocytosis has a female predominance, in contrast with the male predominance observed in Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH) and juvenile xanthogranuloma (JXG).4A comprehensive understanding of ALK-positive histiocytosis requires systemic surveys, leading to further subcategorization into group 1A (multisystem involvement, including the liver, spleen, and hematopoietic systems), group 1B (multisystem involvement, encompassing the nervous systems, lungs, bone, skin, and lymph nodes), and group 2 (single-system involvement).4Of note, group 2 usually involves the skin or nervous systems and often requires surgical removal. ALK-positive histiocytosis and JXG have potential similarities in clinical manifestations and histopathological findings.6,7Both ALK-positive histiocytosis and JXG exhibit positive staining for CD68 and CD163, and lesional tumor cells in ALK-positive histiocytosis are positive for ALK staining.7,8Molecular testing for ALK rearrangements should be performed to confirm the diagnosis of ALK-positive histiocytosis, particularly in patients presenting with multiple lesions with atypical histiocytic proliferation.4,8In addition to the commonly observedKIF5B::ALKgene fusion, documented cases include other gene fusions, includingDCTN1::ALK,CLTC::ALK, andTPM3::ALK.4,8It is noteworthy that patients with ALK-positive staining but no ALK rearrangements may not benefit from ALK inhibition.4In unresectable cases, disease control may require the use of chemotherapy, radiotherapy, and ALK inhibitors, such as crizotinib, alectinib, or lorlatinib.4,8 Cutaneous histiocytoses encompass a diverse group of diseases characterized by the accumulation of cells in the skin exhibiting cytological and phenotypic features of macrophages or dendritic cells.7In LCH, cutaneous lesions typically present as erythematous vesicles, pustules, or papulonodules. Histopathological examination reveals monomorphous, medium-sized histiocytes containing a pink and kidney-shaped nucleus, often accompanied by epidermal exocytosis. Definite diagnosis of LCH relies on positive immunostaining for S100, CD1a, and CD207,7all of which were negative in the present patient. Rosai-Dorfman disease typically manifests as widespread, erythematous to brownish papulonodules in children. Systemic symptoms may occur and include fever, lymphadenopathy, and anemia. Histopathological examination reveals signs of emperipolesis, a feature not observed in the present patient. Immunostaining results for Rosai-Dorfman disease may be positive for S100, CD68, and CD163 and negative for CD1a and CD207.7Erdheim-Chester disease (ECD) typically affects adults, with characteristic cutaneous manifestations of yellow-brown papules or plaques on the face or trunk.1,8,9Classic histopathologic features of ECD include foamy histiocytes with small nuclei, Touton giant cells, and extensive fibrosis, and it is characterized by positive immunostaining for CD68 and CD163 and negative staining for CD1a and CD207.9﻿BRAFV600E alteration may also be present in ECD.8,9 This case outlines a patient presenting with typical clinical and histopathological features of ALK-positive histiocytosis with single-system involvement, as confirmed by positive results for theDCTN1::ALKfusion gene. Treatment options such as vinblastine/prednisolone-based chemotherapy or crizotinib were suggested, but the patient’s family expressed hesitation. Therefore, the patient was treated with prednisolone, 4 mg, twice daily and topical hydrocortisone ointment, with periodic follow-up for outcome evaluation. Although diagnosis of this unique entity is rare, it is critical for physicians to perform a thorough systemic examination and implement appropriate treatment.
